profile.summary: Zephaniah is a short and intense prophecy about the "day of the Lord": a time of real and impartial judgment that strikes Judah, Jerusalem and also the nations. The book confronts false religious security, idolatry, social injustice, greed and arrogance, calling the people to repentance, humility and the Lord's sincere pursuit. At the same time, he announces hope: after judgment, God will preserve and gather a faithful remnant, bringing restoration, purity, joy and lasting peace. To the evangelical reader, the book unites moral seriousness and eschatological hope, pointing to the final justice of God and to the salvation he gives to the humble.
profile.setting: Zephaniah ministered in Judah during the reign of Josiah (640-609 BC), probably at the beginning of that reign, before the discovery of the Book of Law and before the broader religious reforms, which places the prophecy around 635-622 BC. The scenario was of spiritual and social crisis: idolatrous practices inherited from the previous period, religious indifference, the corruption of leaders, injustice, violence and economic exploitation. The introduction suggests that the prophet lived in Jerusalem and knew closely his conditions. As for authorship, there is little information beyond the genealogy in 1:1; the Judeo-Christian tradition usually associates the Zephaniah mentioned there to King Hezekiah, but this is not presented as absolute certainty.

structure.label: Judgment Announced on Judah and Jerusalem
structure.description: Opening with the solemn proclamation of the Lord's day, which reaches the land, Judah and the capital, denouncing idolatry, spiritual apathy and signs of widespread corruption.

structure.label: Call to repentance and judgment upon the nations
structure.description: Exhortation to seek the Lord with humility and justice; then proclaim judgment against the neighboring peoples for their arrogance and opposition to God.

structure.label: Condemnation of Jerusalem and promise of restoration
structure.description: Accusation against the corruption of Jerusalem, followed by the vision of universal judgment and, at the end, of salvation: God removes the arrogant, preserves the remnant and restores his people in joy and security.

themes: The Lord's Day as Holy and Comprehensive Judgment
Moral responsibility of the covenant people before God
Prideness, arrogance and false religious security
Call to humility, repentance, and the Lord's search
Judgment that paves the way for restoration of the remnant
readingKeys: Notice how the book alternates denunciation and hope: the same God who judges also preserves and restores.
Note that Judah is not treated as immune to judgment; the covenant does not eliminate the need for repentance.
Follow the contrast between the proud and the humble, especially in the portrait of the remnant who trusts in the Lord.
profile.cautions: The exact date and genealogical identification of Zephaniah are discussed; the introduction only makes probable a ministry in the early reign of Josiah. It is also important to read the images of judgment as strong prophetic language, whose goal is to call repentance and proclaim God's sovereign justice, not only describe isolated historical catastrophes.

dossier.narratedEra: The book depicts Judah and Jerusalem in the period of King Josiah, with the backdrop of a religious and social crisis prior to the reforms associated with the discovery of the Book of Law (environment of 640-609 BC, especially before 622 BC). The scene also includes the horizon of judgment on neighboring nations such as Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush and Assyria, culminating in the theme of the Lord's Day.
dossier.compositionEra: The source provides two layers of dating: the prophetic setting of Zephaniah lies at the beginning of Josiah's reign, between approximately 635 and 622 BC, before the reforms; the tradition of authorship places him as a prophet of this period, without another firm biographical data. Matthew Henry only says that Zephaniah was the last of the precative minor prophets and puts him just before Jeremiah, without proposing a precise date beyond that framework. The notes also read the prophecy as having long-term reach, with some elements fulfilled in 586 BC, others in other historical episodes and ultimately at the end of time.

politics.title: Transition from Amon to Jewels after anti-assyria instability
politics.detail: The source associates Amon's death, around 640 BC, into the context of an anti-Assyrian revolt in the Near East. After the repression of Asurbanípal, leaders of Judah murdered Amon and put Josiah on the throne.
politics.readingImpact: Zephaniah is a voice at a time of political and moral rupture, when the leadership of Judah is fragile and divine judgment appears linked to the instability of the kingdom.

politics.title: Reign of Josiah as a historical frame of prophecy
politics.detail: Josiah is described as king of Judah for long reign (640-609 BC), initiated at the age of eight, and linked to later reforms after reading the Book of Law.
politics.readingImpact: It helps the reader to place the message before the reforms, when the prophetic denunciation still needed to confront a society without broad reform.

politics.title: Authorities of Judah under strong responsibility
politics.detail: The notes highlight "leaders and princes" as influential officers - civilians, military, tribals or even religious - and put them under special guilt for their corrupt leadership.
politics.readingImpact: It shows that judgment not only affects the people in general, but also the ruling elite, which intensifies the ethical reading of 1:8 and 3:1-4.

politics.title: Regional powers judged: Philistia, Moab, Amom, Cush and Assyria
politics.detail: Zephaniah is presented as an oracle against neighboring peoples: Philistia to the west, Moab and Ammon to the east, Cush to the south and Assyria to the north. Assyria is treated as impending collapsing potency, and Nineveh appears as a symbol of total ruin.
politics.readingImpact: The book not only deals with the internal problems of Judah; it fits the Lord's dayhouse as an international judgment and, at the same time, reverses the expectation that Judah can rejoice at the fall of others without being judged.

politics.title: Dispute of Judah with empires and the logic of retribution
politics.detail: Reading links the violence of empires and neighboring kingdoms to the principle that God judges both nations and their own people. The mention of Babylon appears only as a later realization over Philistine cities (Gaza, Ascalom, Asdode, Ekron), not as the immediate setting of prophecy.
politics.readingImpact: He avoids reading Zephaniah as a simple commentary on a single empire; the focus is on divine sovereignty over all political powers.

customs.title: Skencizing cul up with Baal, Astro, and Moloque
customs.detail: The notes describe idolatrous practices in Judah: idolatrous priests promoting Baal, worship of the sun, moon and stars, and the persistent temptation of the Moloque/Milcom/Baal cult, with explicit prohibition in the Law.
customs.readingImpact: The denunciation of Sophaniah gains weight as a critique of the corrupt daily worship; the problem is not only social, but also a liturgical and theological.

customs.title: pagan rites in the routine of the temple and the city
customs.detail: In 1:9, the note mentions the custom of "pulling the threshold" to avoid contact with the temple, in deference to a pagan god. In 1:10-11, there is reference to foreign traders with broad business in Jerusalem, which suggests visible economic circulation in the city.
customs.readingImpact: It shows that apostasy was not abstract: it was incorporated into religious gestures and concrete urban habits.

customs.title: Economic life marked by foreign trade and elite luxury
customs.detail: The notes note that leaders wore garments from foreign merchants and that there were great commercial ventures in Jerusalem. There is also a complaint of greed that exploits the poor.
customs.readingImpact: The 1:8-13 reading starts to include fashion, consumption and profit as signs of moral corruption, not just as scenario details.

customs.title: Agriculture as an image of urgent repentance
customs.detail: In 2:2, the note depicts farmers threshing cereal in windy hills; the grain and straw were thrown into the air to separate by the wind.
customs.readingImpact: The appeal to seek the Lord appears as a brief and concrete opportunity; the image reinforces the urgency of 2:1-3.

customs.title: Urban desolation converted into pastoral landscape
customs.detail: The prophecy about destroyed cities being reduced to pastures, currals and surrounded for sheep is interpreted as severe punishment. In Nineveh, ruins, obstructed doors and empty windows are images of abandonment.
customs.readingImpact: Helps read judgment as a reconfiguration of everyday life: urban centers have seen empty space, without trade, security or human habitation.

customs.title: humble community and restored remnant
customs.detail: The source speaks of a humble, purified and restored to the earth, living in justice, security and worship of the Lord. This community is opposed to the proud and arrogant who will be removed.
customs.readingImpact: The book is also read as a promise of community reordering, not only of individual punishment.

language.title: "Day of the Lord" as a reversal and cosmic judgment
language.detail: The notes insist that the Lord's day is wider than a local event: it includes destruction, darkness, ruin and, in a certain reading, the reversal of the breeding (gent, animals, birds, fish in reverse order).
language.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Zephaniah uses language of cosmic reach to say that God's judgment dismantles the order of sin and not just a political situation.

language.title: Images of darkness, blindness and moral disorientation
language.detail: The note on 1:15-17 highlights "Darks and darkness," in addition to the image of walking groping like blind, applied to judgment upon the people who were morally and spiritually blind.
language.readingImpact: The language reinforces that the problem of Judah is of spiritual perception; judgment exposes the blindness that the people themselves cultivated.

language.title: Cage of court in 3:8
language.detail: The note describes God as a witness and judge in a forensic scene: He rises, accuses and utters a fair sentence. It also highlights the "fire of my zeal" as the language of the holy divine zeal.
language.readingImpact: Prophecy is not only a warning of disaster, but divine judicial process; this gives legal form to the accusation against nations and Jerusalem.

language.title: "Pura" versus "polluted" Jerusalem
language.detail: The city is called polluted and removed from its vocation as a holy city. The note associates this with the idea of collective infidelity and contrast with the hoped holiness.
language.readingImpact: The urban metaphor brings about holiness and public life: Jerusalem is judged as a city that has lost its identity.

language.title: Vocabulary of the remnant: humility, truth, trust and joy
language.detail: The notes repeat the virtues required of the people: humility, submission, trust in the name of the Lord, truth and fear without arrogance. In 3:14-20 there is an accumulation of imperatives of joy.
language.readingImpact: The language of salvation is not passive; it creates an ethical and devotional profile for those who await the Lord.

language.title: Extensive temporal and eschatological range
language.detail: Matthew Henry reads the book as the last of the pre-cative prophets and as a message with reference to the grace of the gospel; Tyndale's notes also say that parts are fulfilled in 586 BC, others in later times and, finally, at the end of time.
language.readingImpact: The text is read in layers: immediate history, repetition in history and future consummation. This invites you to an evangelical reading that sees judgment and hope united.

timeline.title: End of Amon's reign and the rise of Josiah around 640 BC.
timeline.detail: After the repression of an anti-Sossy revolt, Ammon was murdered and Josiah was placed on the throne of Judah.
timeline.readingImpact: It is the prophecy in a scenario of political transition and institutional fragility, before religious reform.

timeline.title: Reign of Josiah and later reforms around 622 BC.
timeline.detail: Josiah reigned from 640 to 609 BC; in his 18th year the Book of Law was found, and then religious reforms described in 2 Kings 23 and 2 Chronicles 34-35 were found.
timeline.readingImpact: The date suggests that Zephaniah came before that turning point and perhaps prepared the people for reform.

timeline.title: Prophecy located between about 635 and 622 BC.
timeline.detail: The source proposes this range as likely for the prophetic activity, because the practices denounced still remember the period of Manasseh and why the reforms of Josias would have already corrected part of the picture.
timeline.readingImpact: It prevents reading the book as a reaction to reforms; it denounces a previous state, more chaotic and idolatrous.

timeline.title: Partial judgment in 586 BC and later historical echoes
timeline.detail: Tyndale states that part of the passage of 1:7-18 would be fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, and other dimensions would reappear at other historical times, including the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, until the final consummation.
timeline.readingImpact: Helps read the prophecy as containing real historical fulfillment and also repeatable pattern, without reducing the text to a single event.

timeline.title: Fall and ruin of empires and cities as historical signs of judgment
timeline.detail: The notes state the imminent overthrow of Nineveh and Assyria; on the Philistia, they mention the conquest of Gaza and Ascalom by Nebuchadnezzar, as well as the fate of other cities. The ruin of Sodom and Gomorrah is used as a paradigm of permanent judgment.
timeline.readingImpact: It shows that Zephaniah uses concrete historical and geographical examples to announce the seriousness of divine judgment in history.

timeline.title: Final horizon of the Lord's day
timeline.detail: The notes conclude that the Lord's day culminates in eternal blessings at the end of time when God judges and renews creation.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the book gains eschatological closure: judgment is not the last act, but the way to restoration and ultimate joy.

investigation: The historical coverage is selective: the sources concentrate on Judah, Jerusalem, and neighboring nations, with little direct social information beyond what deduces from 1:8-13 and 3:1-4.
The proposed appropriation is broad and supported by the internal reading of the notes; there is no external proof presented here to fix an exact year of composition.
The identification of Hezekiah in 1:1 with the king is traditional, but the source formulates it as probability and not as a demonstrable historical certainty.
Some elements are clearly interpretative, such as the link between Zephaniah and Josiah's reforms, or the reading of certain oracles as repeated in multiple epochs.
Matthew Henry offers a devotional and canonical reading, while Tyndale provides exegetical notes; both were only used when they explicitly inform the text.
No archaeological data, detailed chronologies or etymologies were added outside of what the notes quote directly.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the notes provided and therefore does not intend to reconstruct the complete history of Judah, Assyria or Babylon based on external sources. There are real gaps on the prophet's biography, Jerusalem's administrative structure, detailed economy and popular religious practices beyond the examples mentioned. The policy section includes only rulers, empires and disputes explained in the notes, and the number of customs is limited to habits, worship, work and everyday life actually discussed. Some statements are interpretive tradition (e.g. the identification of Hezekiah with the king and the relationship with Josiah), and others are broad readings of the prophecy itself (multiple and eschatological obligations).
